newsitem.title: UK: Dlr ends lower in Europe on year-end asset jitters.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends lower in Europe on year-end asset jitters.

text.p: The dollar ended down more than one pfennig and one yen here after fresh year-end jitters hit the U.S. stock and bond markets and investors looked to book substantial profits ahead of the Christmas holiday season.
Analysts said the reasons cited for the nervousness in the asset markets were thin, however, and the time of the year was the most influential backdrop.

Despite resurfacing talk of a rise in U.S. interest rates, for example, today's U.S. producer price report for November still showed subdued price pressures there, with the core PPI, excluding food and energy, up a modest 0.1 percent.

"A lot of the overnight excuses for this profit-taking in the asset markets were pretty flimsy but there are some reasons to be nervous at this time of the year and so people are being cautious," said Julian Jessop, economist at Nikko Europe.
At 1630 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.5407/12 marks compared with a close here on Tuesday at 1.5544/51. Against the yen, it was at 112.87/92 compared with 113.27/32 on Tuesday.

A sharp drop in S&P U.S. stock futures overnight in Far East trading fuelled the latest bout of nerves as traders cited a Wall Street Journal story about Japanese investors' increasing wariness of U.S. assets.
"The Japanese story does have some meat on the bone but as far as we're concerned this is only a seasonal concern ahead of the Japanese fiscal year-end (in March)," said Jessop at Nikko.

The uneasiness spilled over into the Dow Jones index, which dropped more than 100 points shortly after the opening, but rebounded later. The benchmark U.S. Treasury bond lost more than one point before steadying.

The dollar found good support below 1.54 marks and bounced off chart support at 1.5370 in afternoon trading. Markets were calmed by the benign PPI report and comments by Federal Reserve board member Alfred Broaddus.
Broaddus said a deceleration of U.S. growth in the fourth quarter was a "good thing" and recent U.S. inflation reports were "very encouraging."

Analysts said that while assets may be unnerved by scattered talk of a Fed rate rise at its policy-making meeting next week, the shift in interest rate expectations in favour of the dollar on both sides of the Atlantic now makes it a buy on dips.

Bank of France monetary policy council member Paul Marchelli re-iterated the growing conviction in France that the dollar remains significantly undervalued versus all European currencies and that French and European interest rates should fall further.
Bundesbank board member Ernst Welteke told a German magazine that while there was no need for a rate cut at present, there was still room for more easing if it was needed.
"It's understandable that the dollar is nervy with asset markets so volatile, but it's hard to see why fundamentally people are selling dollars," said one trader at a Swiss bank.

Some cited yesterday's news of a sharp widening of the third quarter U.S. current account deficit as weighing on the dollar, but the data showed the bigger shortfall was funded by rising demand for dollar assets from private overseas investors, rather than official central bank sources, analysts said.
The weekend European Union summit and EU finance ministers meeting tomorrow are keeping up demand for marks on European crosses and this is capping the U.S. unit.

The risk of a breakdown of negotiations about the post-monetary union budget stability pact is making some investors wary of convergence trades. But analysts believe there will be some form of agreement and more German flexibility than people currently expect. But in Europe too, the approach of the year-end is a major influence as fund managers book profits on European convergence trades before Christmas.
